twoMessages.title: Interlude I: Two Messages
twoMessages.intro: Your cab ride home is a silent affair. Though the two telegrams you hold in your hands both seem to know you were at the Trattoria del Parche the night of the O’Bannion job, their tones couldn't be more different from one another. It’s clear to you that at least one of them—perhaps both of them— can’t be from your original benefactor.
twoMessages.telegram1:
The first message was sent only a day after events unfolded at the Hotel Seasons, written in an uneven hand that is markedly different from the delicate script your original invitation had been penned in. It reads:

Still more to discuss—the worst is yet to come.
Meet Sept 18, Cavalier Speakeasy—Southside.
Have the answers you need.
Password: Tullamore.
—F.
twoMessages.telegram2:
The second message arrived several days into your stay at St. Mary’s. It is professionally typed, and its postmark reveals that it was sent from Boston.

Request your presence at the Parker House Hotel
in Boston on the evening of Sept 18
Please accept apologies for the continued mystery
Importance cannot be understated
Happy you made it out in one piece
—GG
twoMessages.decision: You mull the two messages over. Your curiosity demands answers, but there's no telling who or what is waiting for you at either destination. Either one of these telegrams could end up spelling trouble for you, and you'll only be able to choose one of them to attend. Hopefully, it'll be the right one.
twoMessages.cavalier1:
It takes a bit of time to navigate through the dimly lit alley behind the Saltonstall Street Market before you find the door you need. After a gruff doorman accepts the password from F's message, you are finally welcomed into the Cavalier Speakeasy: a preferred haunt of the O’Bannion gang, tucked neatly away underneath the streets of Southside. There's a small crowd congregating near the bar, swaying to the somber tunes spun by the house jazz band, but the doorman points you to a small booth in the far corner of the room before you can consider joining them.

It takes no time for your contact to sidle up to the booth. The young man slides you a snifter of murky liquor onto the table before settling in across from you, a grim expression of frustration plain on his face. “Hope finding the joint wasn’t too much of a hassle,” the man rasps, and it’s then that you notice the ruddy bandages snaking around his neck. Realization hits you like a truck. Across from you sits the bartender from the Hotel Seasons, the one you last saw bleeding out behind the bar.
twoMessages.cavalier2:
“Finlay O’Doyle,” he croaks, tipping his own ™~ glass back. His voice is understandably hoarse. “Thanks for showing up.” Finlay’s name sticks out like a sore thumb in the conversation; one shared with Declan O’Doyle, the old man at the center of the Hotel Seasons massacre. “Yeah, yeah. My granddad,” he admits with distaste. “I was his watchdog that night, in case things soured. If I'd known the kind of hell he was about to bring down on us with that Mafia cow, I'd have planted him in the ground myself.”

“That lowlife broad’s the heart of this whole mess.” Finlay continues, refilling his now-empty glass from his own flask. “Ana Giuliano. For a while, I thought she was just some wrinkled-up old good-time gal he picked up from Boston. If only I knew what they'd been scheming.” Finlay hits the brakes for a moment, letting the weight of his words hang in the air. “She's the reason granddad split from the crew, and the reason everything's gone down the drain ever since. Miss Naomi’s had to pull up stakes and go into hiding, and I need your help finding her so we can stand a fighting chance.”

You prod Finlay for answers. Why pull you into this mess in the first place? You'd never even met him before the night of the hit. He snorts into his glass. “I wanted you to help me rat out my granddad and Giuliano, of course. In case you weren't aware, you have a rep around this town for fixing hard problems. That's what the dame who answered your phone told me when I gave you that first call—that this was the sort of thing you dealt with all the time.”

Your gut twists into a tight knot. If Finlay’s story is true, he had reached out to you before the Hotel Seasons massacre, but he couldn’t be the one who wrote the mysterious invitation you received. Worse still, that means his message was intercepted by someone who had been inside your house.

“Now don't look so glum, pal,” Finlay says, noticing the expression on your face. “I've got a lead. With your help, we can wrap this up in two shakes. Whenever granddad called Giuliano into town, he'd hole her up in one of our joints. With a bit of luck, we can pick up her scent there.

Then, bing, bang, boom: I take Giuliano for a long walk off a short pier, and you get a nice wad of cash. Sound good?” He stretches a hand across the table, the first signs of a grin on his face. Perhaps this meeting didn't answer all of your questions, but maybe Finlay and his info can help you make some sense of all of this.

You take his hand and shake it.
twoMessages.parkerHouse1:
The train ride from Arkham is mercifully » uneventful. When you step onto the platform at North Station in the heart of Boston’s downtown district, it's just a brisk stroll under the glare of neon lights and streetlamps before you arrive at the Parker House Hotel. Inside, the hotel is every bit a work of art as the Seasons, with polished marble floors and sophisticated French décor. You barely have enough time to give your name to the hotelier before you are intercepted by a tall, broad-shouldered man in a black fedora. “Our guest of honor,” he grunts. “Come.”

The man swiftly leads you to the hotel lounge before taking a post at the doorway, folding his arms menacingly. Inside, a glamorous young woman sits with her back turned to you, idly swirling her champagne in its glass with disaffected elegance as she watches the world outside the window pass by. She cuts a dazzling figure, an effect that is significantly diminished when she takes note of your arrival and opens her mouth to speak. “Thank goodness,” she says, with a nasal voice that could crack solid glass. “You made it. Charmed, I'm sure.”

You don’t have much time for pleasantries, but Giada Giuliano—“Gigi” to her friends—insists on making small talk before she cuts to the chase. You suspect that she’s nervous. “We like to solve our problems in-house, capice?” she sighs, sipping her champagne. “We don’t usually need to look outside the family if we got an issue, but this time...” Gigi explains that she recently got hitched to her long-term boyfriend, but it’s hard not to flinch when you hear her new husband’s name. Mobster Jackie Giuliano is one of the most. feared men in the Boston underground, and his name carries weight wherever it's printed. The implication hangs in the air, and you ask if she contacted you in hopes of being rescued from her new marriage. “What, save me? From my big galoot? Nah,” she laughs. “I need you to save him.”
twoMessages.parkerHouse2:
As you settle into the plush seat across from Gigi, she pulls out a photograph from her clutch and slides it in front of you. You recognize the stately grand dame in the photo—this was the woman holding court at the head of the O’Bannion party's table at the Hotel Seasons.

The woman in the photograph, explains Gigi, is Ana Giuliano—her new mother-in-law. “Six months ago, she showed up on our doorstep unannounced. Jackie was over the moon to see his good ‘ol ma from the old country. Took all of five minutes for her to start acting like she ruled the damn joint, to start filling Jackie’s head with ideas. Ideas like staking bigger claims and sending messages with bullets. Taking out the O’Bannions in Arkham would send a message to all our rivals that no one would be able to cross us and live to tell about it.” You're forced to concede that wiping out the O’Bannions as a show of force has its own dark logic, though you're surprised that the reasoning behind the attack at the Hotel Seasons is so simple. “Yeah, see, that’s the thing,” says Gigi, producing a second photograph from her purse. “It sure ain't.”

The second photograph in front of you is significantly older and faded, featuring a seaside portrait of a young boy with scabbed knees sitting next to a stern, older woman in a plain dress. “Jackie showed this to me when we first got together, and I never forgot about it,” she snarls. “That's Jackie's mother, not whoever this fake is. That's why I need you, understand? Help me figure out how to stop this, how she’s got him fooled, before she sends my baby down a one-way street.”

Side by side, the two women in the photographs look as different as night and day. If Gigi is telling the truth, there's no way that the women in each photo could be the same person. You lean in to ask how she got wind of you, why she invited you to the Hotel Seasons. “My boys told me you're no greenhorn,” she smirks. “Haven't you been solving riddles like this for years? Truth is, I meant to flag you down sooner, but this is the first time I’ve put out a formal invitation.” Gigi pauses to finish off the last of her champagne. “We had to check the papers to see if you even made it through the hotel bloodbath alive. I didn’t toss you into that mess, cross my heart.” The revelation that Gigi isn’t your elusive benefactor is, to say the least, disappointing. She catches the shift in your demeanor and cracks a grin that’s equal parts charm and mischief. “Hey, chin up, honey. I'm not about to toss you into another mess unprepared, neither. I know exactly where Ana’s holed up, and my boys have paved the way for a smooth operation. Plus, we're talking compensation. Big, fat stacks. You get me?”

Whether or not Gigi is entirely trustworthy remains to be seen—she is, after all, the wife of an underworld kingpin—but the identity of Ana Giuliano may be the key to the mystery you're beginning to unravel. It couldn't hurt to dig a little deeper—especially if the pay is right.
twoMessages.finlayAward: Any one investigator may choose to add Finlay O’Doyle: Faithful Watchdog to their deck. It does not count toward their deck size.
twoMessages.gigiAward: Any one investigator may choose to add Gigi Giuliano: Been Things, Seen Places to their deck. It does not count toward their deck size.

label.cavalier: Meet F. at the Cavalier Speakeasy in Arkham.
label.parkerHouse: Meet GG at the Parker House Hotel in Boston.

theRoseOfTuscany.title: Interlude II: The Rose of Tuscany
theRoseOfTuscany.intro:
You're bone-tired by the time you finally get home. The events of the past few days have drained you to the core. Your mind is cluttered with thoughts of Nussbaum Academy and the Three Conies, but you're too fatigued to make much sense of them. By the time you're inside your own room, the relief of returning home is such a comfort that you almost miss the dim glow of the lit cigar in the shadows.

You aren't alone. Your hand moves instinctively to your coat pocket, but a smoky laugh cuts through the silence. “You stop that. It’s bad manners,” says a woman's voice. “And I've been waiting for you all night. Turn your lights on. I'm tired of sitting in the dark.”

When the lights turn on, a stern-looking woman in a shabby coat sits across the room from you, seated in your chair. Dark circles mark her heavy-lidded eyes, and tangled strands of wet hair cascade around her shoulders like a lion's mane. She extinguishes her cigar on your windowsill, ignoring your protestations. “You and I have quite a bit to discuss,” she says, speaking in an accent you can’t quite place. “Sit, now. Time is not a luxury we are afforded.”

Although there is something about this woman's pompous way of speaking that almost compels you to follow her instructions, you're not about to let an intruder dictate terms to you in your own home. You demand to know her identity, what she wants, and how she managed to get inside. “You are inane. How does anyone get anywhere?” she answers blithely, rolling her eyes at you. “How did any of us arrive at this moment? Fate, perhaps? You opened the door and walked inside. It will make you feel better to think that I did, too.” She allows the silence to linger for a long, frustrating moment before she inhales sharply through her nose in exasperation.

“I am Maddalena Talenti,” she declares, in a tone usually reserved for royalty. “You received an invitation to dine at the Hotel Seasons some days ago. I sent this invitation to you. I wished for you to bear witness to the events that are now unfolding.”
theRoseOfTuscany.nameOfTheRose: You've heard that name before. The late American folklorist Charles Godfrey Leland claimed to have learned much of his comprehensive knowledge on witchcraft from an elderly peasant woman in Tuscany named Maddalena Talenti. However, Leland passed over twenty years ago, and the Maddalena he knew would be positively ancient by now. This pompous young woman before you simply does not match up with the woman Leland described.
theRoseOfTuscany.outro:
Suddenly, there is scratching at your window. Behind Maddalena, you glimpse the dark, ominous outlines of birds —ravens, perhaps— beating their wings against the glass in a frenzy. Maddalena’s stern demeanor falters, giving way to a look of genuine fear. “We have been found,” she gasps. “We must go now. We are in grave danger.”

You begin to demand answers to your growing barrage of questions: Who has tracked you down? What is going on, and where is the explanation you are due?

But Maddalena simply presses her thumb against your forehead, and with a single, decisive push, you're sent reeling—and suddenly you are no longer in your room, but somewhere altogether different. A desolate place, draped in darkness, beneath an infinite, starless sky.
theRoseOfTuscany.bonus: Record that your investigator knows the Name of the Rose. You (and only you) gain 2 bonus experience.

label.reader: Choose an investigator to read The Name of the Rose.

theThreeMothers.title: Interlude III: The Three Mothers
theThreeMothers.intro:
The task before you is daunting. To survive their wrath, you must learn all you can about the Three Mothers—the three immortal witches that lie at the root of this mystery. Maddalena’s cryptic explanations of their true nature while you journeyed through The Long Quiet did much to underscore the terrifying scope of their power and sinister goals, but any actual knowledge you have of who they are and what they want from you is frustratingly slim.

Though Maddalena had promised to stay in contact through her familiar, Stolas, you haven't heard a single word from her. The owl itself has been little more than a nuisance, leaving a trail of feathers and filth around your home, but you're not about to let Maddalena’s silence or her pet's poor behavior deter you. With a weary determination, you begin to explore your options.
theThreeMothers.outro: With your new information in hand, you begin tossing essentials into your suitcase. Stolas watches you from his perch on the shelf, tilting his head in that curious way of his. There’s still been no word from Maddalena, but you can't sit around waiting for her. Time’s ticking away, and you have a trio of witches to stay one step ahead of.
theThreeMothers.instructions: Each player must choose a passage that applies to their investigator to begin uncovering the mystery of the Three Mothers.

label.lodge: Civic, Cultist, Entrepreneur, or Silver Twilight
label.theCityOfFog: Travel to San Francisco: The City of Fog.

label.aChorusOfSuffering: Travel to the Gulf of Naples: A Chorus of Suffering.

passages.police:
With the O’Bannion Gang and the Boston Mob butting heads, your contacts at the Arkham Police Department are stretched thin trying to keep peace on the streets. One alarming report stands out amongst the others as you search through the precinct’s records; a mirror image of the murders that followed in the wake of the Hotel Seasons’ fire are playing out in real-time on the streets of San Francisco, clear across the country. The victims, all mowed down in classic gangland style, all have one thing in common: a membership to the Tenebrarum Lodge, a local gentleman's club. You swallow the lump in your throat. Tenebrarum. That can’t be a coincidence. With a quick glance over your shoulder, you stash the report away in your coat pocket.

Record in your campaign log that you learned about the Tenebrarum Murders. Add 1 copy of Tenebrarum’s Favor to your deck. This card does not count toward your deck size.
passages.armitage:
When you decide to seek out the wisdom of your dear friend Dr. Henry Armitage, the head of Miskatonic University’s Orne Library, he is delighted to oblige. He arrives at your doorstep carrying a stack of heavy books, which he deposits in your arms with a grunt. “Thomas de Quincy's Suspiria de Profundis should be a fair jumping off point,” Armitage wheezes, wiping his brow with a handkerchief. “But after that, you'll want to delve into Our Ladies of Sorrow by Brother Ross.”

You find that Suspiria de Profundis is mostly poetic drivel, waxing lyrical about the Three Mothers in vague, flowery prose. It paints them as metaphors for human suffering, rather than actual entities, and provides little in the way of concrete information. Brother Ross’s book is an entirely different beast. A sixteenth-century account by a Welsh monk scrawled on delicate, yellowed pages, Our Ladies of Sorrow is a detailed collection of historical events that Ross claims are the devilish work of the Three Mothers. “The Sorrows, or Our Ladies of Sorrow, are dreadful spirits from the dawn of man, ageless and endless. They may be daughters of Lilith, although they sometimes exhibit a compassion for mankind that the Queen of Night lacks. Or they may be kin to grim Hecate, though they do not shun the daylight as she does. They may be three, or they may merely be one. There are hundreds of legends about them, in their multitude of forms. Which of these stories are closest to the truth is anyone's guess.”

Record in your campaign log that Dr. Armitage taught you about the Three Mothers. Reveal tokens from the chaos bag until a {cultist}, {tablet}, or {elderThing} is revealed. If a {cultist} was revealed, add Tenebrarum’s Favor to your deck. If a {tablet} was revealed, add Suspiriorum’s Favor. If an {elderThing} was revealed, add Lachrymarum’s Favor. This card does not count toward your deck size.
passages.dream:
You dreamt in vague, abstract nightmares that night. You recall standing at a crossroads, and that you felt a heavy, dragging sense of loss—the sensation of drowning deep in some great body of water, clawing for air that wouldn't come. The only other thing that you've managed to retain from your dreamlike haze is the memory of sitting beneath a majestic chestnut tree on top of a hill, staring out across a moonlit bay.

It’s not until later the next day, when you stumble upon a photograph in one of your books, that it suddenly all clicks. The hill with the tree, overlooking the ocean—your dreams had taken you to the faraway Gulf of Naples in Italy. You don’t know why, but somehow, you're absolutely certain that you'll find a key to unlocking this mystery in that very bay.

Record in your campaign log that you had a prophetic dream. Add 1 copy of Lachrymarum’s Favor to your deck. This card does not count toward your deck size.
passages.academy:
The clinking of glasses and the hum of lively conversation fill the smoky air of the Cavalier speakeasy. You've been nursing a glass of whiskey at the bar for half an hour when the conversation you've been eavesdropping on takes an intriguing turn. “Can you believe it?” one of the two women says, leaning in conspiratorially to her friend. “After all these years, Madame Nussbaum is going back to Germany. Who will run the school, I wonder?” You feign disinterest, but your mind is racing— Helena Nussbaum, the elusive and mysterious headmistress of Nussbaum Academy, should have known about the coven of witches you found deep in the bowels of her school... it stands to reason that she would be a link back to the Three Mothers as well.

The other woman, clearly drunk, chides her friend. “Don't be stupid, Suzy. Madame Nussbaum never leaves Freiburg. Madame Pappenheimer runs the school in her place. Everyone knows that.” You lean back, letting their words sink in. This is more than idle chatter— this is a lead.

You polish off the last of your drink. Perhaps it’s time for you to pay Helena herself a visit.

Record in your campaign log that you learned where to find Helena Nussbaum. Add 1 copy of Suspiriorum’s Favor to your deck. This card does not count toward your deck size.
passages.finlay:
Finlay leans back against the worn leather armchair, his face etched with lines of exhaustion. “Listen,” he croaks, still recovering from the wound to his neck. “We've been digging into Giuliano’s affairs, trying to piece together her connections and her motives. Turns out, a good chunk of the change from her recent dealings was going straight into someone else’s pockets.” He takes a drag from his cigarette, his eyes fixed on yours. “An opera star over in Europe named Amalia Verdi. Seems like Giuliano was funneling funds her way for some reason. Don't know what the connection is, but something tells me it ain’t just for love of the music.”

Record in your campaign log that you discovered Ana Giuliano’s connection to Amalia Verdi. Add 1 copy of Lachrymarum’s Favor to your deck. This card does not count toward your deck size.
passages.gigi:
A dim light casts shadows across Gigi’s face, accentuating the worry lines spreading into her features as she frets over her missing beau. “So, my boys dug up something interesting during our little tête-à-tête with Mother Darling,” she begins. “Seems like every last dime she pinched from us found its way into funding some grand opera over in Italy. Mother Darling has been bankrolling productions starring a girl named Amalia Verdi. I'll call it like I see it: Mother Darling’s no patron of the arts, and if she’s been spending this much coin on Verdi, the girl’s rotten.” Gigi sighs and recedes into her seat, pouting. “Of course it’s Italy. Always is. I’m never gonna get to see Paris, am I?”

Record in your campaign log that you discovered Ana Giuliano’s connection to Amalia Verdi. Add 1 copy of Lachrymarum’s Favor to your deck. This card does not count toward your deck size.
passages.lodge:
Given recent events, you can’t help but feel extremely apprehensive when you find a new, black envelope slipped under your doorway. You wonder if mysterious invitations will start becoming a daily annoyance.

You rip it open to reveal several train tickets bound for San Francisco, along with a brief, cryptic message: “You are cordially invited to join the Tenebrarum Lodge.” The name can’t be a coincidence, and you don’t like the implication one bit. It’s a risky lead—but it’s exactly what you need to start untangling the mystery Maddalena has left in her absence.

Record in your campaign log that you were invited to join the Tenebrarum Lodge. Add 1 copy of Tenebrarum’s Favor to your deck. This card does not count toward your deck size.
passages.mandel:
A nagging suspicion has been gnawing at the back of your mind ever since you lost contact with Maddalena. You can’t shake the feeling that you've heard of something like this before. You're reminded of an account you heard of long ago, during your training: something about a veteran, returned from the war, but what was it? Driven by instinct, you arrange to visit the department of records at Arkham Sanitarium. It’s only a few hours into your search before you find the dusty records on Patient #84762: Sergeant Frank Mandel.

You thumb through the pages, and pieces of the puzzle begin to fall into place. Sgt. Mandel had been a decorated soldier, but he had returned from his post near Freiburg im Breisgau, Germany, as a man shattered.

His file is a catalogue of horrors, filled with sketches of spectral figures and twisted corpses rendered in a trembling hand. Your heart quickens as you turn to the final entry in Mandel’s diary. It’s all here—the same dread, the same sense of impending doom that hangs heavy above your own head.

“Ever since we met in the Black Forest, I see her all the time. I hear her terrible whispers. My own secrets revealed to me, and hers as well.

Mother. All she wants, she says, is to be embraced, loved. Known.

But to know her is to give up my soul. God, forgive me.

She claims to grieve, but her sorrow is a knife.

She claims to love, but her love is the abyss.

suspiriorum’

Record in your campaign log that you read Sgt. Mandel’s file. Add 1 copy of Suspiriorum’s Favor to your deck. This card does not count toward your deck size.
passages.kaslow:
The door to the fortuneteller’s shop creaks open. Inside, the air is thick with the smell of incense, and the old fortune teller behind the table fixes you with a knowing look. “Yes, yes. I know why you've come, of course,” Anna Kaslow drawls. “Snooping around where you shouldn't, as usual. Well, sit down. Make yourself comfortable. It might be your last chance.” Anna begins to lay out her tarot cards, arranging them in a complex pattern. The three cards at the center catch your eye - the Queens of Swords, Pentacles, and Cups. A smirk plays on the old woman's lips. “Now that you've crossed paths with the three queens, they won't be letting you off easy. Seen or unseen, they'll be on your tail, meddling with your dreams. Start nudging you down paths you wouldn't dream existed. If the queens are fond of you and you dance for them well, you might make a darling pet. It’s not the worst deal in the world, you know.” Somehow, you aren't surprised that the old fortune teller knows about the Three Mothers, but the nonchalance with which she suggests that you might end up under their spell is unnerving. Undeterred, you ask Anna if she knows of anything that can help you. “Help you? What makes you think I can do anything to help you?” the fortune teller replies, her tone flat. “Curse them, curse your fate, make your peace with God. Once they've got their sights on you, your life is forfeit. If you're lucky, they might become bored with you and consign you to a hole somewhere—like an old toy. Otherwise, you're bound to ‘find out why they call themselves Sorrows.”

There’s a moment in the silence that lingers afterward that you begin to resign yourself to your terrible fate, but Anna laughs, and her eyes soften. “... Or so they like to say. Stories do have power of their own. But stories twist with every telling, and old women like me tend to have their own tales to tell—and scores to settle. So why don't you let old Anna tell you a story about exactly where you might find her oldest, dearest friends?”

Record in your campaign log that Anna Kaslow directed you toward an old colleague. Reveal tokens from the chaos bag until a {cultist}, {tablet}, or {elderThing} is revealed. If a {cultist} was revealed, add Tenebrarum’s Favor to your deck. If a {tablet} was revealed, add Suspiriorum’s Favor. If an {elderThing} was revealed, add Lachrymarum’s Favor. This card does not count toward your deck size.

theThreeMothers.chooseDestination: The investigators must choose a destination to continue their investigation.

ourLadiesOfSorrow.title: Interlude IV: Our Ladies of Sorrow
ourLadiesOfSorrow.intro: A jolt in the tracks snaps you awake. You stare groggily into the night outside, unable to make anything out in the darkness but your own reflection. After weeks of travel and contending against the Three Mothers, you've begun to feel just how much these trials have been chipping away at your spirit, bit by bit. The chaos left in the wake of the Tenebrarum Lodge killings, the disappearances in the Black Forest, that rain-drenched world where time seemed to have no meaning—each surreal encounter has left its mark on you. Since Maddalena’s last cryptic letter, there’s been no word, no clue as to what might have become of her. You can only hope that she’s safe, working in secret to prepare against the Three Mothers and what they have in store for you. But without direction, and with no leads to follow, you've resigned yourself to a long journey back to Arkham. It may be the only place left to prepare for whatever lies ahead.
ourLadiesOfSorrow.finlay:
If the past few weeks have been hard on you, they've stripped Finlay to the bone. In the wake of the horrors you've experienced, you've watched the once-strapping young man become a shadow of himself: gaunt, pale, and sickly. You've tried to broach your concern, but each time he’s brushed it away with a tired smile. “I'm fine,” he continues to insist. “I'll have time to rest once this is all over.” Now, as the train groans to a halt in the dead of night, you peer out the window into an endless darkness. No lights, no signs, nothing to hint at why you've stopped—so it comes as a surprise when Finlay rises to his feet. “This is my stop,” he says, his voice low and dreamlike. “Thanks... for everything. I really mean it.” He slides the cabin door open, his movements calm and dreamlike, and steps into the narrow corridor.

Something awakens at the back of your mind—a memory from Freiburg; the tories of the villagers wandering, hypnotized, into the night. Alarmed, you scramble after him, catching sight of Finlay just as he reaches the door at the end of the car, He turns to offer you one last, weary wave before stepping off.

You rush after him and fling open the door—and find only an endless, inky void, stretching as far as the eye can see. Finlay is nowhere to be seen, and gone with him are the solid ground, the night sky, and the rest of reality.
ourLadiesOfSorrow.gigi:
The train rattles along, lulling you into a half-stupor as you lean back in your seat. Gigi dozes across from you, her purse perched in her lap. There's a pang of something akin to sympathy stirring within you. You expected she'd be nothing but trouble from the start—and she’s done everything in her power to prove you right—but seeing her now, after everything you've endured together, Gigi’s tenacity in the face of everything she’s lost almost seems noble. You shut your eyes, ready to drift back asleep— and then Gigi’s shrill, piercing scream breaks the silence.

You spring upright, ready to bolt into action, but there is simply none to be had. There’s no sign of a struggle, no shadowy assailants. Gigi is simply gone, with only the agonizing sound of the train to punctuate her scream. Her purse lies abandoned on her seat, the only trace that she'd ever been there at all. You throw open the compartment door to find help, but as you face the window across the corridor, dread coils in your chest like a snake. Outside the train, there is only an infinite void. No solid ground, no stars, no horizon—just a dark, yawning nothingness that stretches into eternity.
ourLadiesOfSorrow.outro:
It’s tempting to give in to the sense of panic rising in your throat, but you swallow it down. You'd known that the Three Mothers would come for you eventually; Maddalena had said as much, after all. You just hadn't expected it to be here, in this strange limbo you find yourself in now.

‘It's very good of you to stay calm. They mean to hurt you, now.” A dark, husky voice cuts through the quiet. You turn, and there she i Maddalena Talenti, lounging in your cabin as if conjured from thin air, a lit cigar balanced between her lips. Stolas hops from his perch on your luggage to land on her shoulder. ‘You've made fools of them,” she continues, her tone laced with dry approval. ‘And for that transgression, they harm those closest to you. So, well done. I couldn’t be prouder of you.” You sink back into your seat. Maddalena’s sudden, timely appearance is all the assurance you need to understand that this long journey is nearly at its end.

She takes a drag of her cigar and exhales, rings of smoke curling lazily in the ceiling. “Now that the Three Mothers have stolen you back into the Astral sea,” she begins, and there's a hint of fondness for you in her voice that wasn’t there before. “I can now intervene. They mean to drag you to the seat of their power, where they believe—falsely—that it will be a simple thing to unmake you. I intend to be there to make them understand their error.”

And where exactly are you being pulled to? A smirk curls at the corner of her lips. “It’s a very vain thing they've named it,” she replies, leaning back into her seat, as if it were hers all along. “But you, of all people, should not be surprised by the vanity of the Three Mothers. Not now, after everything you've seen. You will laugh, I think—we go to their home: the Palace of Sorrows.”

If your survival truly hinges on Maddalena’ ability to back up her boasting, who is she to command such power? And if she can stand before the Three Mothers as an equal—what, or who, does that make her? Despite these questions, a strange kernel of resolve blooms within you. You're ready to end this; to stand before the Sorrows, to break free of this twisted ordeal and resume a normal life.

As if such a thing is even remotely possible anymore.
